newsitem.title: UK: Dollar eases vs yen after peak, but outlook strong.
newsitem.headline: Dollar eases vs yen after peak, but outlook strong.

text.p: The dollar sank back against the yen by the European midsession on Friday after a long-awaited stab at 120 yen in earlier trade, but many saw this as merely a correction before the currency reached for higher levels.

After poking above 120 yen for the first time in 47 months, the dollar was driven down by talk of Bank of Japan intervention and consternation over contradictory comments about the yen by senior Japanese government officials.

"We're seeing quite an adjustment in the dollar this morning, but I'd say it was purely a healthy correction. In the longer term, the dollar still has room to rise further," said one dealer at a U.S. bank in London.
The dollar had subsided to 118.77/82 yen by 1230 GMT after hitting a high of 120.15 yen, falling below Thursday's late European level of 119.54/59.

Although the dollar was not expected to make further headway against the yen for today, analysts said economic fundamentals were all pointing towards dollar strength and that it would need more than rhetoric from Japanese officials to turn it around.

"Something that would really affect dollar/yen would be some really strong data out of Japan or some weak data out of the U.S. - that would be a fundamental cause for a turnaround," said IBJ International senior analyst Roger Francis.
"But it looks like it's going to be very difficult to break the declining impetus of the yen. All the signals coming through are saying the Japanese economy is very weak," Francis said.

The market got plenty of rhetoric from Japan earlier, and traders and analysts said the fact that several officials came out to express worries about yen weakness immediately after the dollar hit 120 yen showed how concerned Tokyo was about the currency's speedy decline.

The dollar's rise earlier was sparked by a comment from the Japanese Economic Planning Agency that the yen's weakness was not having a big negative impact on the economy. But when the dollar hit 120 yen, a finance ministry official said Tokyo would not welcome an excessively weak yen, while Japan's chief government spokesman said he was confident the yen would not drop below the 120-yen level.
"Japanese officials have made lots of comments about excessive yen weakness, but they've never actually said what that meant," said Lehman Brothers foreign exchange economist Francis Breedon.

"But now that they've mentioned the 120-yen figure, they will try very hard to protect it. It would be unfortunate for them if the yen went very far beyond that level, because that would reflect on their credibility," Breedon said.
Reports that the Bank of Japan was intervening in the market capped the dollar's momentum. Analysts, however, said it would need hard-hitting words or action from the U.S. to turn it around.
Even though an unlikely scenario, an opportunity for this could arise during U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's speech at an awards ceremony in Washington D.C. at 1800 GMT today.

"I'm not sure the markets will get anything (from Rubin). So far it's all going according to plan, since Rubin has always said a strong dollar is favourable," said Breedon. He added, and others agreed, that there was no reason for great concern about dollar/yen's current level from the U.S. point of view.

Meanwhile, the dollar was steady at lower levels against the mark, with traders saying it was in a consolidation phase. It was at 1.6285/95 marks at 1226 GMT against its late Thursday level of 1.6393/96. The mark was firmer against most other European currencies.
